week.description: AG-UI: the Agent-User Interaction Protocol. Bring Agents into Frontend Applications.
week.readme: AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications. Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent.

The next session starts with a short index of what matters, and pulls in the details only when it needs them. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 11 more agents.

month.description: Browser automation CLI for AI agents
month.readme: Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

new.description: Leonida Is A Native PC Recompilation Of The Xbox Version Of Grand Theft Auto 6
new.readme: Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series) running natively on Windows, built on your PC from your own copy. Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this happens on your PC, from your own copy of the game.

new.description: Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behavior at every step. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries in TypeScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby and Java.
new.readme: Rewrite your app in Rust, and prove it still behaves the same. Point it at your app: it records what the original does, your coding agent writes the Rust one piece at a time, and every piece is checked against that recording before it moves on. It doesn't translate code; it proves the rewrite. Prettier against its Rust port on 59 real files from ms, Fuse.js and json-server (Apple M4). Same output, byte for byte. How it was measured . PHP and C#: record, replay and the front door today; unit ports come next.

Vendor apps usually aren't required: most drivers query devices directly.

new.description: Agent skill for hill-climbing local LLM serving speed (decode, speculative decoding, prefill, KV, startup, TTFT) on any hardware and quantization
new.readme: An agent skill for hill-climbing the speed of a local LLM server on any hardware and any quantization. It covers: single-user and concurrent decode startup time and time to first token It works under a memory cap, and every result has to survive a full-context stability check. It encodes how we actually got these speedups. It is not a list of flags. The workflow: Compute the theoretical ceiling. Measure against interleaved controls. Log every result, including the failures. Gate on long-context retrieval.

new.readme: Xbox2Windows researches static recompilation from Xbox Series X|S (Scarlett) to x64 Windows. new.readme: tiny-voca is a small English text-to-speech model. It has two voices, 4.5M parameters, and runs on a CPU or in the browser. Small: 4,537,291 parameters, 18 MB, waveform generator included. Fast: about 70x real time on four CPU threads. Two voices: F2 (female) and M2 (male), American English, 24 kHz. Runs anywhere: PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, and ONNX Runtime Web. Open: code, weights, training recipe and dataset. Trained from scratch. Long text is fine. It is read one sentence at a time and the audio is joined.

new.description: Yab, yet another browser: a fast native macOS browser with an iPhone and Android companion
new.readme: Yet another browser. A small, quiet browser for the Mac, with an app for iPhone. Yab is a browser with nothing in the way: a row of tabs, across the top or down the left, and the page. One field takes addresses and searches. Pages run on WebKit, the engine inside every Mac, or, on Apple silicon, on Chromium, per tab or per site. Agents from the AI providers you already pay for can work in tabs of their own, and never see a private tab. One field. Type an address and you go there; type words and you search.

new.description: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.
new.readme: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow. Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible. Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup). --agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin.

constraints.note: Official actions with a document that make AI harder, slower or costlier to train, publish, host, reach or buy. New ones first, then those with a date still ahead or seen in the last week; every action stays in the register at data/v1/constraints.json. Magpie reports the mechanism, not the politics.

gap.method: Lag is how long before the open model's release a closed model first reached the same Capabilities Index score. Today's figure measures from that closed model to today, so it grows until an open model moves the frontier.

hardware.finding: GeForce RTX 5090 decodes fastest; DGX Spark fits the biggest models
hardware.method: Ceiling = memory bandwidth / 16 GB of weights; real decode runs below it. Fits = 80% of memory at 0.55 GB per billion parameters (4-bit). List prices are the maker's own store; street prices are dated checks of a major retailer.

possibilities.title: Security teams can roll out bug-hunting agent skills with leak-safe settings enforced centrally
possibilities.why: Claude Code now applies an organization's settings from the Enterprise Admin Console at sign-in, Claude-BugHunter packs 82 bug-hunting skills into Claude Code, and the earlier finding of passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files from a permission shortcut shows which setting to lock first.

possibilities.title: Compliance teams can run always-on regulatory watchers without a hosted scraper
possibilities.why: Pi Durable shows how to build always-on agents with local models, Firecrawl Local scrapes on your machine, and context-mode trims tool output so long-running sessions do not drown in page text.

possibilities.title: Consultancies under client NDAs can serve more local coding agents per DGX Spark
possibilities.why: The OpenCode LoRA lifts local Qwen3.8-27B at about one eighth the tokens, Spark Attic frees about 2 GB more KV cache on headless DGX Sparks, and DSpine speeds the same base model, so each box can carry more concurrent agent sessions.

possibilities.title: Draft models trained on base weights may lose speed on harness-tuned adapters
possibilities.why: DSpine reports 2.3x to 3.2x throughput for Qwen3.8-27B agent replays, but today's pi LoRA changes that model's outputs, so the draft model's guesses may be accepted less often.

possibilities.title: Remote Claude Code fleets in AWS get a learning loop that lowers cost
possibilities.why: Claude Code on Bedrock AgentCore runs isolated remote sessions with no cost figures, and TokenEconomizer learns from repository sessions to cut cost, so a fleet working the same repositories feeds the plugin more sessions to learn from.
